chapters.n: Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament, written perhaps around 450 BC, after the temple was rebuilt. The people’s early enthusiasm had faded into routine and doubt. The book unfolds as a series of dialogues: God speaks, the people object, and God answers.

f.g: A weighty prophetic message.
Means “my messenger” — perhaps a name, perhaps a title (see Malachi 3:1).

chapters.n: God begins with love: “I have loved you.” But the people ask, “How have You loved us?” As proof, God points to His choice of Jacob over his twin, Esau.
“I hated Esau” is a Hebrew idiom meaning “I chose Jacob rather than Esau” for the covenant role — not personal hatred. Edom, Esau’s nation, had been devastated.

f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “loved less” or “did not choose,” as in Genesis 29:31 and Luke 14:26.
Jackals.

chapters.n: Edom vows to rebuild, but God says He will tear down whatever they build. They will be known as a wicked land under God’s lasting displeasure.

f.w: They shall build, but I will throw down

chapters.n: Israel will see this and declare that the Lord is great even beyond Israel’s borders.
God confronts the priests: a son honors his father and a servant his master. If I am your Father and Master, where is My honor? They ask, “How have we despised Your name?”

f.w: if then I be a father

chapters.n: They offer defiled food on God’s altar and treat the Lord’s table — the altar — as if it doesn’t matter.

f.g: Unacceptable offerings; “bread” means food in general.
The altar.

chapters.n: They offer blind, lame, and sick animals — rejects nobody else wants. Would your governor accept such a gift? God deserves our best, not our leftovers.

f.w: if ye offer the blind for sacrifice

f.g: The Persian-appointed governor of Judah.

chapters.n: Go ahead and ask God for favor — but with offerings like these, will He accept you?

f.w: this hath been by your means
f.g: You did this — you are responsible.

chapters.n: God wishes someone would just shut the temple doors rather than keep lighting useless fires on His altar. He won’t accept their half-hearted offerings.

f.g: Close the temple gates — stop the meaningless worship.
In vain.

chapters.n: Meanwhile, from sunrise to sunset God’s name will be great among the nations, and pure offerings will be given to Him everywhere. Ironically, outsiders may honor God more than His own priests.

f.w: from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same

chapters.n: But you profane God’s name by saying His altar and its food are contemptible.

f.g: Treated as common; dishonored.

chapters.n: They complain, “What a bore!” and sniff at worship. They bring stolen, lame, and sick animals. Should God accept that?

f.g: Sniffed in contempt; turned up their noses.
Mauled by wild animals — or taken by robbery.

chapters.n: Cursed is the cheat who vows a good male animal but sacrifices a blemished one instead. God is a great King, honored even among the nations.

f.g: Awe-inspiring, revered.

chapters.n: The Lord addresses the priests directly with a warning.

f.g: This decree or warning.

chapters.n: If they won’t listen and honor God’s name from the heart, He will turn their blessings — perhaps the priestly blessings they pronounce — into curses. It has already begun.

A shocking image: God will rebuke their descendants and smear their faces with the refuse from their own festival sacrifices, and they will be carried out with it. Their unworthy worship will disgrace them.

f.g: The offal from sacrificed animals, normally burned outside the camp (Exodus 29:14).

chapters.n: Then they’ll know God sent this warning to keep His covenant with Levi, the priestly tribe.

f.w: my covenant might be with Levi

chapters.n: God’s covenant with Levi brought life and peace, given because Levi reverenced God.
A portrait of a true priest: he taught truth, spoke no lies, walked with God in peace and uprightness, and turned many from sin. A model for every teacher of God’s word.

f.w: did turn many away from iniquity

chapters.n: A priest’s lips should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from him, for he is the Lord’s messenger.

f.w: the priest's lips should keep knowledge
the messenger of the LORD of hosts
f.g: Hebrew mal’ak — the same word as in Malachi’s name.

chapters.n: But these priests have left the path, caused many to stumble by their teaching, and corrupted Levi’s covenant.

f.w: ye have caused many to stumble

chapters.n: So God has made them despised before the people, because they showed favoritism in applying the law.

f.g: Showing favoritism; bending rules for some.
Lowly, humiliated.

chapters.n: Don’t we all have one Father? Didn’t one God create us? Why then betray one another and break our ancestors’ covenant? A foundation for treating everyone as family.

f.w: Have we not all one father?

f.g: Act faithlessly; break faith. The word appears five times in verses 10–16.

chapters.n: Judah has been unfaithful — profaning God’s holy place and marrying women who worship foreign gods. This drew people away from the covenant.

f.w: married the daughter of a strange god

chapters.n: God will cut off anyone who does this from Israel’s community, no matter who they are, even if they bring offerings.

f.g: Literally “he who wakes and he who answers” — meaning everyone, without exception.

chapters.n: They flood the altar with tears and wailing because God no longer accepts their offerings — but they don’t see why.

f.w: covering the altar of the LORD with tears
f.g: Perhaps also the tears of wives they had abandoned.

chapters.n: Here’s why: God witnessed the marriage covenant they made with the wife of their youth, and they betrayed her. She is your partner and your covenant wife. God takes marriage covenants seriously.

f.g: Marriage is a covenant made before God.

chapters.n: Didn’t God make husband and wife one, with a portion of His Spirit? Why one? Because He seeks godly children. So guard your spirit and stay faithful to your wife. A difficult Hebrew verse, but its message is clear.
The Lord says He hates divorce, and the one who abandons his wife covers himself with violence like a garment. Guard your heart and don’t break faith.

f.g: “Putting away” means divorcing — here abandoning a faithful spouse.

chapters.n: You’ve wearied the Lord with your words. How? By claiming evildoers are good in God’s eyes, or asking, “Where is the God of justice?” This cynical question sets up God’s answer in chapter 3.

f.w: Ye have wearied the LORD with your words
Where is the God of judgment?

chapters.n: God answers “Where is the God of justice?”: He will send His messenger to prepare the way, then the Lord will suddenly come to His temple. Jesus identified John the Baptist as this messenger; the D&C applies it to the latter days too. The Savior quoted Malachi 3–4 to the Nephites.

f.w: shall suddenly come to his temple
Behold, I will send my messenger

chapters.n: But who can endure His coming? He is like a refiner’s fire that burns away impurities, and like a launderer’s strong soap that scrubs clean.

f.w: who may abide the day of his coming?

f.g: Strong lye soap used by fullers to whiten cloth.

chapters.n: Like a refiner patiently watching silver in the fire, He will purify the priests so they offer righteous offerings. Latter-day revelation connects this to the restoration of the priesthood and temple work.

f.w: he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver

chapters.n: Then the offerings of Judah and Jerusalem will please the Lord, as in the good old days.

f.w: as in the days of old

chapters.n: God will come near in judgment as a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, liars, those who cheat workers of their wages, and those who oppress widows, orphans, and foreigners.

f.w: oppress the hireling in his wages

chapters.n: “I am the Lord, I change not.” Because God is constant and faithful to His covenant, Jacob’s descendants have not been destroyed.
Ever since their ancestors’ days they have strayed from God’s ordinances. “Return to Me, and I will return to you.” But they ask, “How shall we return?”

f.w: Return unto me, and I will return unto you

chapters.n: Will a person rob God? Yet you rob Me. How? In tithes and offerings. Tithing means giving a tenth back to God, who gives us everything.

f.g: A tenth of one’s increase, given to God.

chapters.n: The whole nation is under a curse because of robbing God.

f.w: Ye are cursed with a curse

chapters.n: A famous promise: bring the full tithe to the storehouse so there is food in God’s house, and test Him — He will open the windows of heaven and pour out blessings beyond your capacity. One of the few places God invites us to “prove” Him.

f.g: Temple storerooms for tithes (Nehemiah 10:38; Nehemiah 13:12).

f.w: open you the windows of heaven

chapters.n: God will stop the “devourer” — pests like locusts — so crops are not destroyed and vines don’t drop fruit too early.

f.g: Locusts or other pests destroying crops.

chapters.n: All nations will call them blessed, and the land will be delightful.
“Your words have been harsh against Me,” says the Lord. They ask, “What have we said?”

f.g: Hard, harsh, arrogant.

chapters.n: You’ve said, “Serving God is useless. What do we gain by obeying Him and walking around in mourning?”

f.w: It is vain to serve God

f.g: Going about in sackcloth — showing outward penitence.

chapters.n: “The arrogant are the happy ones; the wicked prosper and even test God and get away with it.” A common complaint when life seems unfair.

Then those who reverenced the Lord talked together, and He listened. A book of remembrance was written before Him for those who honored His name. God notices and records the faithful. Adam’s family kept a book of remembrance too.
“They will be Mine,” says the Lord, “My treasured possession on the day I act, and I will spare them as a father spares a son who serves him.”

f.g: Hebrew segullah — a special treasure, God’s own possession.

chapters.n: Then you will again see the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between those who serve God and those who don’t. Justice will be visible.

f.w: discern between the righteous and the wicked

chapters.n: The day is coming that will burn like a furnace; the proud and wicked will be like straw, left with neither root nor branch — no ancestors or descendants. Moroni quoted this to Joseph Smith with slight changes. (Malachi 4 is chapter 3 in Hebrew Bibles.)

f.g: Dry straw left after harvest — burns quickly.

chapters.n: But for those who reverence God, the Sun of righteousness will rise with healing in His wings (rays). They will leap for joy like calves released from the stall. Christians see Christ as this rising Sun.

f.g: “Wings” can mean the rays of the sun — or the corners (fringes) of a garment.
Calves let out of the stall, leaping with energy.

chapters.n: The righteous will tread down the wicked, who will be like ashes underfoot on that day.

f.w: ashes under the soles of your feet

chapters.n: Remember the law God gave Moses at Sinai (Horeb). The Old Testament closes by pointing back to the covenant.

f.g: Another name for Mount Sinai.

f.w: Remember ye the law of Moses

chapters.n: God promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day of the Lord. Elijah appeared on the Mount of Transfiguration, and on April 3, 1836, he appeared in the Kirtland Temple and restored the sealing keys.

f.w: I will send you Elijah the prophet

chapters.n: Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers and children to each other, lest the earth be struck with a curse. Latter-day Saints understand this as the work of sealing families together across generations through temple ordinances.

f.w: he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children
smite the earth with a curse
f.g: Moroni’s version: the whole earth would be “utterly wasted” at His coming — the purpose of creation would be lost without sealed families.
